governance_posts.description:
Summary

LlamaRisk recommends the following parameter changes based on user behavior, on-chain liquidity, and position health observed in the latest review of Aave V4 reserves.

Aave V4 Ethereum:

  • Increase the draw cap for USDC on the Core Hub Main Spoke from 36M to 40M.
  • Increase slope1 for USDC on the Core Hub from 5.00% to 5.50%.
  • Decrease slope1 for USDC on the Prime Hub from 5.00% to 4.50%.
  • Increase the draw cap for USDT on the Core Hub Main Spoke from 15.6M to 20M.
  • Increase the draw cap for WETH on the Core Hub EtherFi Spoke from 41.1K to 45K.
  • Increase the add cap for weETH on the Core Hub Main Spoke from 22K to 25K.

Aave V4 Avalanche:

  • Increase the add cap for USDt on the Core Hub Main Spoke from 60M to 110M.
  • Increase the draw cap for USDt on the Core Hub Ethena Ecosystem Spoke from 50M to 100M.
  • Increase the add cap for USDe on the Core Hub Ethena Ecosystem Spoke from 60M to 120M.
  • Increase the add cap for WAVAX on the Core Hub Main Spoke from 2M to 4M.

Cap Utilization

The chart shows add cap utilization (left) and draw cap utilization (right) for Aave V4 reserves at or above 50% of either cap, split by hub. The draw cap panel excludes cross-hub credit lines, which are draw-only legs through which a spoke borrows from a hub against collateral supplied on another hub.


Source: LlamaRisk, November 3, 2026

USDC (Core Hub)

USDC Main Spoke Borrow Distribution


Source: LlamaRisk, November 3, 2026

USDC borrowing on the Main Spoke is moderately concentrated, with the largest position holding approximately 15% of the drawn amount and the top twenty approximately 60%. The largest borrowers hold USDC debt mainly against ETH-denominated collateral (wstETH, WETH, and weETH) and BTC-denominated collateral (WBTC and cbBTC) at health factors between 1.16 and 3.64 with a median of 1.48, so HF in the cohort tracks the ETH and BTC prices.

Recommendation

As of November 3, 2026, USDC sits at 95.1% draw cap utilization on the Main Spoke (34.25M / 36M). The proposed draw cap of 40M lands at approximately 85.6% post-change draw cap utilization, and the 5.75M of added room is within the 5.94M of USDC liquidity available on the Core Hub.

USDC IRM (Core Hub)

USDC on the Core Hub holds 56.50M added and 50.56M drawn as of November 3, 2026, for a hub utilization of 89.5% against an optimal usage ratio of 92.00%. The proposed change raises slope1 (rateGrowthBeforeOptimal) from 5.00% to 5.50%. The optimal usage ratio (92.00%), base rate (0.00%), and slope2 (20.00%) remain unchanged.

At current hub utilization, the USDC borrow rate moves from 4.86% to 5.35% and the supply APY, after the 10% liquidity fee, from 3.99% to 4.40%. Borrow incentives currently reduce the USDC borrow APR on the Core Hub by 2.00%, so the borrow rate net of incentives moves from 2.86% to 3.35%.


Source: LlamaRisk, November 3, 2026

Recommendation

Increasing slope1 for USDC on the Core Hub from 5.00% to 5.50% raises the supply rate for USDC depositors, while the 2.00% borrow incentive keeps the net borrow rate at 3.35% at current utilization.

USDC IRM (Prime Hub)

USDC on the Prime Hub holds 7.23M added and 6.42M drawn as of November 3, 2026, for a hub utilization of 88.8% against an optimal usage ratio of 92.00%. The proposed change lowers slope1 (rateGrowthBeforeOptimal) from 5.00% to 4.50%. The optimal usage ratio (92.00%), base rate (0.00%), and slope2 (20.00%) remain unchanged.

At current hub utilization, the USDC borrow rate moves from 4.83% to 4.35% and the supply APY, after the 10% liquidity fee, from 3.94% to 3.54%.


Source: LlamaRisk, November 3, 2026

Recommendation

Borrow incentives are not live on the Prime Hub as of November 3, 2026. Decreasing slope1 for USDC from 5.00% to 4.50% reduces the USDC borrow rate at current utilization by 0.48 percentage points.

USDT (Core Hub)

USDT Main Spoke Borrow Distribution


Source: LlamaRisk, November 3, 2026

USDT borrowing on the Main Spoke is moderately concentrated, with the largest position holding approximately 9% of the drawn amount and the top twenty approximately 60%. The largest borrowers hold USDT debt mainly against WETH, WBTC, and wstETH collateral at health factors between 1.30 and 13.32 with a median of 1.73, so HF in the cohort tracks the ETH and BTC prices.

Recommendation

As of November 3, 2026, USDT sits at 92.5% draw cap utilization on the Main Spoke (14.42M / 15.6M). governance_posts.title: 2025 Events Recap
governance_posts.description:
Greetings Aave Community,

We’re happy to publish this report with our events activity 2025, walking you through the activities we have organized and the results they yielded this year.

2025 has been a huge year for Aave, and we’re happy to report that the momentum and strength of the brand have come through in our live appearances. Our regular followers keep coming back for more, while we continue to add new partners to DeFi Day. For Cannes we welcomed four new sponsors into the community, and five out of the total twelve partners were onboarded for the Buenos Aires edition. We also captured the interest of existing and future integration partners, institutional targets and more.

The Aave brand strengthens every year and continues to be known for complementing the protocol’s growth, high-quality track record and lasting power. Buenos Aires was home to our rAAVE #13 and our fourth DeFi Day, and both events were sold out.

Cannes

We hosted two full days at a hillside villa with a wide view of the coast. It became home to meetings, our two flagship events (DeFi Day and rAAVE), and a V4 demo for the Aave DAO. The Aave villa was a standout during EthCC and became a destination on its own.

DeFi Summer Day

In Cannes, at DeFi Summer Day, attendance hit record numbers, with more than 2,600 people waitlisted and over 600 attending. Sponsors included Chainlink, Sky, Ethena, Etherfi, Certora, Chaos Labs, Aptos, ZKsync, Fireblocks, and more. Our panels picked up the pulse of the moment, covering stablecoins, RWAs, interop, and blockchain modularity. Speakers included Vitalik Buterin, Sergey Nazarov, Guy Young, Avery Ching, and many more.

The programming attracted partners from across the Aave ecosystem, ranging from crypto natives to institutional users, who were excited about the future of the Aave Protocol, Horizon, and GHO.

rAAVE Cannes

For rAAVE, we leaned into the Cannes vibe and turned the Aave villa into an all-white disco. The stage was set outdoors, with LED screens showing hand-drawn Ronnie animations. As usual, the door was packed, hitting capacity the entire night, and the energy was high.

We launched a new merch shop, this time featuring the coveted rAAVE pieces. A bar facing the ocean served cocktails, soft drinks, and wine. We watched the sunset from the deck to Max Menaged, who opened the night. The dancing carried on with Antdot’s tropical grooves, Alma Linda, and closing with an incredible combo, Jamiie b2b Xenobi. rAAVE Cannes was a success, drawing even media attention on CNBC.

The Cannes Merch Collection

Aave events wouldn’t be complete without custom, high-quality merch. For Cannes, we took inspiration from nautical elements from the French Riviera. We made embroidered t-shirts and linen pants, colorful polo shirts, and more. Crochet hats, fans, and totes were new additions for rAAVE, and the ultra-soft Aave and GHO socks made a comeback.

EthCC Booth and Talks

Aave has always made it a point to support Ethereum France, which has consistently given us speaking slots at the conference and backed the brand from early on. We had a booth for the first two days, where Aave Labs engineers and business development teams met with builders and community members, explored new opportunities, and gathered user feedback.

In addition to it, Stani got to introduce Aave v4 on the main stage, and later on Emilio offered a deep dive on the upcoming upgrade’s innovative architecture.

Ronnie Film Festival by Metamask

Aave was invited by Metamask to host a custom experience for the week. In collaboration with Metamask, we created the Ronnie Film Festival, a one-day event that took Aave friends on a journey with macaron tastings, helicopter rides, and more.

Guests filmed their day, spent together with Ronnie, the Aave mascot, and the best clips were chosen by a jury and awarded trophies, in true Cannes style.

The activation helped launch the Metamask Card and spotlight the successful Linea Aave market.

London

DAS London DeFi Brunch with Galaxy and Blockchain.com

In October, we hosted over 80 people at the Aave Labs office for a brunch co-hosted with Galaxy and Blockchain.com. DAS (Digital Asset Summit) gave us a strong moment to grow Aave’s presence across institutions and real-world assets.

Buenos Aires

Devconnect Argentina

Aave Labs took over the DeFi District at La Rural, the venue for Devconnect Argentina. As usual, the booth had lines throughout the week. We used the spotlight to announce the Aave app waitlist, powered by Aave V3, while keeping focus on V4 awareness and business development.

Our top engineers joined the event, along with a video team capturing interviews and content to grow our presence on Instagram and TikTok.

Across the six days of Devconnect, Aave Labs spokespeople appeared across multiple stages:

  • Stani shared the new Credit architecture at Ethereum Day, joined Manuel Beaudroit for a fireside chat at Crecimiento’s Startup World Cup, and spoke on stablecoins at the Ethereum Foundation’s DeFi Today.

  • Mario Baxter Cabrera (Director of Product) introduced the Aave App at the World Fair stage: DeFi’s “iPhone moment.”

  • Mark Hinschberger (Senior Engineering Manager) presented Aave Pro, the new web app coming to aave.com.

  • Dhairya Sethi (Staff Engineer, Smart Contracts) and Tomer Ganor (Security Lead at Certora) walked through Aave V4’s security blueprint at the DeFi Security Summit.

Buenos Aires was also a fertile ground for us to ramp up our marketing video strategy efforts: several months ago, we had already started deploying the Smart Money series on Aave’s Instagram and TikTok, as well as short clips from the Cannes DeFi Day talks. In Buenos Aires we recorded vox pops, deep dives into Argentinian economy and how stablecoins are helping people deal with inflation, interviews, and more. This footage is currently being edited and posted.

DeFi Day Del Sur

The fourth edition of our flagship event took place on November 19, 2025, at La Escondida de Palermo in Buenos Aires. This time, we aligned with Devconnect’s goal of cementing the city as the crypto capital of Latin America.

We invited the founders of Lemon, Belo, Ripio, and Sovra.io to share how they’re driving regional adoption. All but Sovra have integrated Aave, collectively reaching more than 9 million users across LATAM.

Integrations overview:

  • Lemon has used Aave since 2021, with 4 million users across Argentina, Peru, and Colombia.

  • Ripio integrated in 2022. Its products reach 25 million people across Latin America, with 4 million app users mainly in Argentina and Brazil.

  • Belo serves over 1.5 million users in 20 countries, with a strong presence in Argentina and Brazil.

We co-hosted the event with 1inch, CoW DAO, Uniswap, Optimism, Aptos, Avalanche, Chainlink, Sky, kpk, Chaos Labs, Upshift, and Linea. Over 600 guests joined panels on commerce, stablecoins, DeFi innovation, RWAs, and more. We also brought back the fan-favorite merch shop with caps, t-shirts, tote bags, and other items.

rAAVE Buenos Aires

rAAVE Buenos Aires lit up Palacio Alsina, drawing over 1000 guests for a full night of music and celebration. Custom LED visuals brought Ronnie, flowers, and psychedelic animations to life. The crowd danced to B2B sets from Max Menaged, Jamiie x Julya Karma and Gallivanter x Xinobi, and an electric live performance by Sinego.

Buenos Aires Merch Collection

For our Buenos Aires merch, we took a deep dive into Argentinian icons. We drew from 70s Argentine music and its psychedelic art, added playful sketches of Ronnie drinking mate, and placed Aave next to Maradona, the Argentine iconoclast, under the title Los Mejores Del Mundo (the best of the world).

BD Dinner at Madre Rojas

On November 17, 2025, we took over Madre Rojas in Buenos Aires to host dinner for 50+ current and future partners and integrators.

As a final note, we’re pleased to confirm that the 2025 events strategy, which included careful budget allocation and partnering with top tier projects to co-finance the events, has resulted in $214,189 unspent funds that are being carried over towards the 2026 events.

2025 brought new momentum and helped reinforce Aave’s place in DeFi as crypto expands again. The Aave Labs events team thanks the DAO for the trust and support that made this year’s events possible.

Aave Labs

2025 brought new momentum and helped reinforce Aave’s place in DeFi as crypto expands again. The Aave Labs events team thanks the DAO for the trust and support that made this year’s events possible.

governance_posts.title: [TEMP CHECK] Aave Protocol Treasury Revenue Sharing Program
governance_posts.description:
Author: AxieAur

Title: Aave Protocol Treasury Revenue Sharing Program

Date: 2026-04-07

Abstract:

Initiate and implement AAVE Protocol Treasury Revenue Sharing Mechanism. Create mechanism to share monthly AAVE protocol revenues with stakers of AAVE token who have been staking for 30 or more days. Start monthly revenue share at .25% of Aave protocol monthly revenues. Users will be able to claim revenues from frontend dashboard.

Motivation:

The intent of this initiative is multi-faceted:

  • Create direct and long-term alignment between AAVE’s protocol profitability and AAVE token investors

  • Encourage further staking of $AAVE, taking coins out of circulating and reducing available supply

  • The idea of earning cash yield is more attractive than earning tokens for many investors

  • Signal to market and investors owning $aave means owning a part of the protocol revenue. The amount isn’t as important as the philosophical direction and signal. Investors will want to own a piece of the revenues from the largest decentralized borrow/lend protocol in the world especially as we scale into securing trillions of dollars

  • Add new value lever to AAVE token that can be increased or decreased dynamically based on company position, market conditions, etc… to increase the value proposition for $aave holders. Implement now while things are slow

Specification:

Each month:

On the first day of each month, .25% of Aave’s monthly revenues are made claimable to stakers of $AAVE who have staked for over 30 days (claim proportionate to user’s staked AAVE > 30 days / total staked AAVE > 30 days)

aave monthly revenue * (.0025) * (user’s stkaave amt > 30 days / total stkaave amt > 30 days) = user’s share of monthly revenue

This program can work in tandem with buybacks and/or buybacks can be eliminated if appropriate. Both have their pros and cons, and may be appropriate in different situations. There may also be situations where it makes sense to use neither.

The percentage of distribution is very small by design due to Aave’s current growth stage. There are trillions of dollars of value to be captured, and growing into the trillions of dollars secured is the most important goal. It is important the vast majority revenues focus on growth.

1 out of 400 dollars earned shared with stakers leaves 99.75% of revenues to be used for growth. Revenues shared in today’s environment would be very small.

Next Steps:

  • Collect community feedback, conduct discussion, iron out technical implementation path if idea is well received

Copyright is open source on this proposal

Summary

LlamaRisk recommends the following parameter changes based on user behavior, on-chain liquidity, and position health observed in the latest review of Aave V3 reserves.

Aave V3 Core:

  • Reduce borrow cap for USDG from 100,000,000 to 24,000,000.

Aave V3 Arbitrum:

  • Increase borrow cap for USDC from 172,000,000 to 200,000,000.

  • Increase borrow cap for USD₮0 from 39,400,000 to 45,000,000.
  • Increase borrow cap for WETH from 56,500 to 65,000.
  • Increase borrow cap for WBTC from 149 to 250.

Aave V3 Base:

  • Increase supply cap for cbETH from 60,000 to 70,000.
  • Increase borrow cap for WETH from 79,900 to 90,000.
  • Increase borrow cap for USDC from 178,000,000 to 195,000,000.

Aave V3 BNB:

  • Increase supply cap for ETH from 10,000 to 12,500.
  • Increase supply cap for BTCB from 1,200 to 1,500.
  • Increase borrow cap for WBNB from 4,000 to 6,000.

Aave V3 Mantle:

  • Reduce supply cap for USDC from 60,000,000 to 25,000,000.
  • Reduce borrow cap for USDC from 54,000,000 to 22,500,000.

Aave V3 Monad:

  • Reduce supply cap for AUSD from 40,000,000 to 20,000,000.
  • Reduce borrow cap for AUSD from 32,000,000 to 16,000,000.

Aave V3 Plasma:

  • Increase borrow cap for USDe from 30,700,000 to 35,000,000.

Aave V3 Polygon:

  • Increase borrow cap for USDT0 from 23,000,000 to 30,000,000.
  • Increase borrow cap for USDC from 18,000,000 to 25,000,000.

Aave V3 X Layer:

  • Increase supply cap for USDe from 50,000,000 to 75,000,000.

Partial Reversal of October 30, 2026 Borrow Cap Reductions

The borrow caps below were reduced on October 30, 2026. We recommend raising each to a level below its pre-reduction cap. Figures are as of November 4, 2026.

  • cbBTC (Aave V3 Core): from 149 to 250. Cap utilization moves from 87.2% (130 / 149) to approximately 52.0%, and the proposed cap corresponds to 1.4% reserve utilization at current supply, below the 80.00% optimal point.

  • USDC (Aave V3 Arbitrum): from 172,000,000 to 200,000,000. Cap utilization moves from 96.3% (165,630,578 / 172,000,000) to approximately 82.8%, and the proposed cap corresponds to 97.6% reserve utilization at current supply, above the 90.00% optimal point.

USDC Slope1 Increase (Aave V3 Arbitrum)

Instance Asset Utilization uOptimal Current Borrow APR New Borrow APR Delta

USDC on Aave V3 Arbitrum carries a lower Slope1 than the 4.50% applied to many stablecoin reserves across Aave V3, including USD₮0 on the same instance. cbETH Supply Distribution

Recommendation

We recommend raising the supply cap from 60,000 to 70,000 on Aave V3 Base, landing at approximately 79.6% post-change cap utilization.

ETH Supply Distribution

Debt is concentrated, with the largest borrower holding approximately 40% and the top three approximately 71%, and the borrowers shown run HF between 1.14 and 3.09 with a median of 1.74. Fifteen post BTCB and eight post ETH as collateral.

We recommend raising the borrow cap from 4,000 to 6,000 on Aave V3 BNB, landing at approximately 66.4% post-change cap utilization.

USDe sits at 22.9% supply cap utilization (11,441,881 / 50,000,000) on the Aave V3 X Layer instance as of November 4, 2026. The reserve carries no outstanding debt against its 10,000,000 borrow cap and acts as collateral only inside the USDe Stablecoins E-Mode (LTV 91.00%, LT 93.00%).

Source: LlamaRisk, November 4, 2026

Supply is concentrated, with the largest supplier holding approximately 76% and the top three approximately 98%. Four of the top five suppliers carry debt at HF between 1.02 and 1.03, borrowing USD₮0, USDC, and USDG against USDe.

Recommendation

We recommend raising the supply cap from 50,000,000 to 75,000,000 on Aave V3 X Layer, landing at approximately 15.3% post-change cap utilization.

LlamaRisk recommends the following parameter changes based on user behavior, on-chain liquidity, and position health observed in the latest review of Aave V4 reserves.

governance_posts.title: Strategic Proposal for Establishing a Standalone Innovation Lending Market for AAVE
governance_posts.description:
Strategic Proposal for Establishing a Standalone Innovation Lending Market for AAVE

Core proposition: While advancing V4 development, V4 shall not serve as an innovation testbed. Leverage battle‑tested V3 to launch the standalone AAVE Innovation market parallel to AAVE Core. Innovation handles asset incubation, risk rating and screening; Core admits fully‑validated high‑quality assets, mitigating depositor‑confidence risks unresolved by V4 Hub‑Spoke.

I. The Need for a Standalone Innovation Market

Innovative assets deliver limited protocol yields yet carry severe tail risks threatening the core liquidity pool, as demonstrated by rsETH and tBTC incidents. Even well‑audited collateral bears external risks from underlying protocols, cross‑chain bridges and redemption logic. V4’s Spoke limits and emergency halts only cap book losses and cannot stop depositor panics and bank‑run risks. Therefore, insufficiently battle‑tested assets must be barred from direct access to the core unified liquidity pool.

II. Two‑Market Division & Asset Promotion Rules

AAVE Core: Supports ETH, BTC, mainstream stablecoins and fully‑audited graduated assets via a unified liquidity pool with strict admission criteria, prioritizing retail and institutional depositor safety.

AAVE Innovation: Deployed on modified V3 codebase as a Morpho‑comparable isolated lending venue with fully independent liquidity, decoupled from Core’s shared Hub. It hosts unproven collateral: liquid‑staking derivatives, cross‑chain wrapped assets and emerging RWA. Assets undergo a 12‑24‑month reference testing cycle covering real liquidations, oracle stress, extreme‑market liquidity, underlying‑dependency security and bad‑debt handling. Approved assets enter Core with incremental small‑size limits. Innovation‑market access does not guarantee Core promotion; DAO risk governance retains full review authority for this scarce credit resource.

III. Addressing Morpho & Phoenix Competition, and Fee Framework

Morpho is AAVE’s most formidable DeFi‑lending rival, rapidly capturing market share by courting curators, niche‑collateral issuers and sophisticated traders through its permissionless curator architecture. Phoenix likewise expands into niche lending segments. Both aggressively compete for innovative collateral, institutions and advanced users.

Morpho’s flexible curator system is its key strength yet creates a critical structural flaw: it does not operate a deep, unified and trusted core‑liquidity hub. While rivals offer risk‑isolated markets, they lack AAVE‑scale unified liquidity and the full‑cycle loop: asset incubation → stress testing → access to top‑tier liquidity. This constitutes AAVE’s distinctive edge, which Morpho’s curator‑only design cannot replicate.

AAVE Innovation applies low, transparent protocol fees. Projects may opt out, yet will forfeit eligibility for AAVE Core liquidity unless they complete Innovation‑stage trials and comply with risk rules. Fee‑paying participants obtain lending infrastructure, AAVE user exposure, third‑party‑audited risk ratings, live stress‑test environments and the exclusive promotion pathway into Core. Curators and issuers face a clear trade‑off: Morpho delivers isolation flexibility at the cost of AAVE’s brand power and deep core liquidity. DAO governance sets modest fees to avoid stifling innovation. A multi‑dimensional risk‑rating system replaces pure APY‑based sorting to clearly communicate market‑level risks to end‑users.

IV. V4 Alignment & Overall Outcomes

This proposal complements rather than rejects V4. V4 Hub‑Spoke optimizes capital efficiency for mature‑asset Core operations. Innovation stays independently on V3 with strict fund‑risk‑loss isolation and no forced migration into V4 shared Hub.

Three core outcomes: contain tail‑risk spill‑over to safeguard Core depositors against rsETH‑ / tBTC‑style shocks; generate sustainable DAO revenue; build durable competitive moats via the closed loop: Innovation discovers and validates assets; Core absorbs proven mature assets.

governance_posts.title: Streaming yield for Aave depositors and app savers
governance_posts.description:
Hi Aave community,

This is Amin from Superfluid. Superfluid powers continuous settlement for tokenized markets and the agentic economy.

We’re exploring where Superfluid could add value to Aave. We think that as yield becomes commoditized, the cashflow experience can become a differentiator for some users. Most savers might make an initial decision based on the APY. But they might not build an ongoing habit around it.

Superfluid can make yield become a visible real-time stream. A stream of money arriving every second feels different to a balance that changes from time to time. That inbound stream representing the yield can be used as income or redirected to other products on the platform. Here is a live technical demo of streaming yield from a Morpho vault: SuperVault. More on streaming yield here.

Could streaming yield be a useful option for Aave depositors and Aave App Savings users?

Appreciate any feedback from the Aave community.

governance_posts.title: The Literacy Barrier in DAO Governance: How Technical Complexity Excludes the Global South
governance_posts.description:
Context

This post is not about a specific proposal. It is about a pattern I have observed over years of DAO governance research and experienced personally.

I am sharing it here because Aave is one of the most important governance communities in DeFi. If this conversation can happen anywhere, it should happen here.

The Core Observation

DAO governance presents itself as open and decentralized. But in practice, two invisible filters determine whose voice carries weight:

1. Token Concentration
Governance power flows to whoever holds the most tokens. Early insiders and protocol teams accumulated tokens before most of the world knew these protocols existed. Communities across South Asia, Africa, and Latin America were never part of that early accumulation.

2. Technical Fluency
Risk proposals arrive as multi-page documents filled with LTV ratios, oracle thresholds, and slippage curves written to demonstrate expertise, not to inform the community. When the bar for “valid participation” requires understanding 40-parameter risk tables, most people quietly conclude they have nothing to say.

Together, these filters make exclusion feel like a personal failing not a structural problem.

Data as Armor

There is a difference between using data for transparency and using complexity to avoid accountability.

When a service provider exits abruptly without community consultation, without a public post-mortem, without explaining what conflict triggered the departure and the community’s only response is another technically dense proposal, that is not transparency. That is the appearance of rigor being used to move past uncomfortable questions.

The real governance questions require no PhD:

  • Who decided this?
  • Was there a conflict of interest?
  • What accountability exists for damages to ordinary users?
  • What changes will prevent this next time?

What I Experienced Personally

When I raised carefully researched questions about a powerful service provider on this forum, my comment was placed on a 24-hour hold. On separate occasions, posts were removed. Across multiple governance forums, I have faced holds lasting months.

The stated reason: my questions could “affect a billions-dollar protocol.”

A community member asking a researched governance question was considered a risk. Not the abrupt vendor exit. Not the wrongful liquidations. Not the damages to ordinary users.

The question was the problem.

That is not community protection. That is insider protection.

India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Sri Lanka hundreds of millions of people with genuine reason to care about decentralized finance are largely absent from governance. Not because they lack intelligence or interest. Because these systems were built by and optimized for a specific group and the barriers to participation were never designed to be removed.

What Genuine Inclusion Would Look Like

  1. Plain-language summaries mandatory for all proposals before voting proceeds
  2. Moderation transparency — all holds/removals publicly logged with stated reasons
  3. Conflict of interest disclosure — service providers must declare financial relationships before commenting on their own proposals
  4. Regional representation in delegate structures — structural commitment, not optics
  5. Community accountability layer — independent of technical teams, focused on process fairness

Closing

The most consequential risk in DAO governance today is not a miscalibrated oracle.

It is the quiet, sustained removal of voices that ask why.

Decentralization without inclusion is not an achievement. It is a rebrand.

Context

This post is not about a specific proposal. It is about a pattern I have observed over years of DAO governance research and experienced personally.

I am sharing it here because Aave is one of the most important governance communities in DeFi. If this conversation can happen anywhere, it should happen here.

The Core Observation

DAO governance presents itself as open and decentralized. But in practice, two invisible filters determine whose voice carries weight:

1. Token Concentration
Governance power flows to whoever holds the most tokens. Early insiders and protocol teams accumulated tokens before most of the world knew these protocols existed. Communities across South Asia, Africa, and Latin America were never part of that early accumulation.

2. Technical Fluency
Risk proposals arrive as multi-page documents filled with LTV ratios, oracle thresholds, and slippage curves written to demonstrate expertise, not to inform the community. When the bar for “valid participation” requires understanding 40-parameter risk tables, most people quietly conclude they have nothing to say.

Together, these filters make exclusion feel like a personal failing not a structural problem.

Data as Armor

There is a difference between using data for transparency and using complexity to avoid accountability.

When a service provider exits abruptly without community consultation, without a public post-mortem, without explaining what conflict triggered the departure and the community’s only response is another technically dense proposal, that is not transparency. That is the appearance of rigor being used to move past uncomfortable questions.

USDt (Aave V3 Avalanche)

USDt has reached 99.9% borrow cap utilization on the Aave V3 Avalanche instance.

Borrow Distribution


Source: LlamaRisk, November 5, 2026

The top 20 USDt borrowers run health factors between 1.19 and 2.95 with a median of 1.85, and borrowing is dispersed, with the largest borrower at about 5% of outstanding debt. 15 of the 20 post BTC.b as collateral and 5 post WETH.e, so HF in the cohort tracks the BTC and ETH prices.

Recommendation

We recommend raising the borrow cap from 22.8M to 30M on Aave V3 Avalanche, which places the reserve at approximately 75.9% post-change borrow cap utilization.

USDC (Aave V3 Avalanche)

Borrow Distribution


Source: LlamaRisk, November 5, 2026

Recommendation

We recommend raising the borrow cap from 64.6M to 70M on Aave V3 Avalanche, which places the reserve at approximately 89.5% post-change borrow cap utilization.

Borrow Distribution


Source: LlamaRisk, November 5, 2026

Recommendation

We recommend raising the borrow cap from 17,000 to 19,000 on Aave V3 Prime, which places the reserve at approximately 86.0% post-change borrow cap utilization.

Supply Distribution


Source: LlamaRisk, November 6, 2026

Supply is concentrated, with the largest supplier holding about 75% of the reserve and the top 5 about 83%.

Borrow Distribution


Source: LlamaRisk, November 5, 2026

The top 20 USD₮0 borrowers run health factors between 1.03 and 1.33 with a median of 1.06, and the largest borrower accounts for about 30% of outstanding debt. 18 of the 20 post PT-USDG-25FEB2027 as collateral.

Recommendation

We recommend raising the supply cap from 100M to 150M and the borrow cap from 70M to 135M on Aave V3 X Layer, which places the reserve at approximately 21.9% post-change supply cap utilization and 20.3% post-change borrow cap utilization.

Source: LlamaRisk, November 6, 2026

Recommendation

We recommend raising the borrow cap from 63M to 70M on Aave V3 Monad, which places the reserve at approximately 81.9% post-change borrow cap utilization.

Source: LlamaRisk, November 6, 2026

The top 7 USDe suppliers hold all of the supply, with 6 of 7 carrying debt at health factors between 1.02 and 1.05 and a median of 1.03. Supply is concentrated, with the largest supplier at about 76%, and the debt is denominated entirely in stablecoins (USD₮0, USDC and USDG).

  • EURC on Aave V3 Core sits at 42.8% supply cap utilization (39.4M / 92M), with supply down 4.5% over the past 30 days. The proposed cap of 55M lands at approximately 71.6% post-change cap utilization.
  • USDS on Aave V3 Core sits at 9.9% supply cap utilization (4.96M / 50M) and 3.1% borrow cap utilization (1.05M / 34.2M), with supply down 42.9% and borrows down 83.7% over the past 30 days. governance_posts.title: [TEMP CHECK] Extend HyperLend's Friendly Fork Recognition to Elysium (Aave v3.7)
governance_posts.description:
Author: HyperLend Team
Date: 2026-11-06

Summary

This proposal seeks Aave DAO recognition of a new HyperLend deployment as a friendly fork of Aave, on Elysium, Kinetiq’s Layer 2 for the Hyperliquid ecosystem.

The deployment will use the Aave v3.7 codebase and will consist only of Aave pools. HyperLend will share 50% of all revenue generated by the Elysium deployment with the Aave DAO. The remaining 50% will be used to buy back HyperLend’s token, HPL.

Block Analitica will continue to serve as risk manager.

Motivation

HyperLend’s track record

In early 2025, the Aave DAO recognized HyperLend as a friendly fork on HyperEVM (TEMP CHECK, ARFC). Since then, HyperLend has:

  • Originated approximately $2B in loans (Block Analitica dashboard)

  • Reached a peak total market size of over $900M (Block Analitica dashboard), and currently holds over $530M in TVL with $250M in active loans (DefiLlama)

  • Operated securely and at scale for more than a year

  • Worked continuously with Block Analitica on risk management

We believe this record shows HyperLend can run an Aave-based money market responsibly. We want to bring that experience to a second network.

Why Elysium

Elysium is a high-throughput Arbitrum Orbit L2 built by Kinetiq. It settles to HyperEVM, runs co-located with HyperCore, and uses HYPE as gas. It is designed for higher-frequency onchain activity than HyperEVM can support.

As liquidity and trading activity grow on Elysium, demand for a reliable money market will follow. HyperLend intends to capture that flow, and this proposal ensures the Aave DAO shares directly in it.

Benefits to the Aave DAO

  • 50% of all revenue from the Elysium deployment, with no exclusions, compared with 10% under our original HyperEVM terms

  • Expansion of the Aave codebase into the Hyperliquid L2 ecosystem with no DAO capital or operational burden

  • An operator with an established track record, an existing relationship with the DAO, and a continuing risk partner

Specification

We propose that HyperLend:

  • Deploy Aave v3.7 on Elysium as a friendly fork operated by HyperLend

  • Offer only Aave pools on Elysium (no isolated pools, P2P, or other products)

  • Share 50% of all revenue generated by the Elysium deployment with the Aave DAO, distributed either monthly or through a RevenueSplitter contract

  • Use the remaining 50% of Elysium revenue to buy back HPL

  • Retain Block Analitica as risk manager for the Elysium deployment

  • Deploy as soon as this proposal passes governance

No token allocation is included in this proposal. The revenue share is the DAO’s compensation.

In return, the Aave DAO should:

  • Grant HyperLend a license to use the Aave v3.7 codebase on Elysium

  • Notify HyperLend of potential security issues in the Aave codebase so they can be mitigated before public disclosure

Next Steps

  1. Gather feedback from the Aave community

  2. Escalate this proposal to a Temp Check Snapshot

  3. If the Temp Check passes, publish an ARFC forum post and escalate to an ARFC Snapshot

  4. If the ARFC passes, deploy on Elysium

governance_posts.title: [TEMP CHECK] AAVE SECURITY SHIELD – Exploring Preventive Risk Controls for External Security Incidents
governance_posts.description:
AAVE SECURITY SHIELD

Propuesta comunitaria para reforzar la prevención de riesgos externos y la protección de los depositantes

Tipo: Iniciativa comunitaria para discusión y evaluación preliminar
Área: Seguridad, gestión de riesgos y resiliencia financiera
Estado: Borrador conceptual previo a una posible ARFC
Autoría: Iniciativa comunitaria independiente
Solicitud inicial: Evaluar el interés de la comunidad en financiar o realizar un estudio de viabilidad, sin aprobar todavía modificaciones del protocolo.

PARTE I. PRESENTACIÓN DE LA INICIATIVA

1. Resumen ejecutivo

La pregunta que queremos plantear a la comunidad de Aave es:

¿Cómo puede Aave limitar la generación de nueva exposición crediticia durante un incidente de seguridad externo, sin perjudicar innecesariamente a sus usuarios?

AAVE SECURITY SHIELD es una iniciativa comunitaria que propone estudiar una capa adicional de prevención, complementaria a los mecanismos de seguridad, gestión de riesgos y respuesta a emergencias existentes en el protocolo.

El objetivo es investigar si determinados controles pueden proporcionar a Aave más tiempo para verificar una amenaza y contener su impacto antes de que se acumule una exposición significativa.

La iniciativa propone evaluar mecanismos que permitan:

  • Identificar amenazas externas mediante señales verificables y criterios transparentes.
  • Limitar temporalmente la generación de nueva deuda cuando exista un riesgo material.
  • Preservar, siempre que sea técnicamente seguro, la devolución de deuda, las liquidaciones y las aportaciones de garantía destinadas a reducir riesgos.
  • Mantener la privacidad y evitar restricciones basadas únicamente en asociaciones indirectas entre carteras.
  • Establecer facultades de emergencia limitadas, supervisadas y sujetas a revisión.
  • Evaluar la capacidad de absorción de pérdidas y las posibles brechas de cobertura.

Entre las alternativas que podrían estudiarse se encuentran los límites a la velocidad de endeudamiento, la habilitación gradual de capacidad crediticia y los periodos de maduración selectiva de nuevas garantías.

No se propone imponer una espera universal de 24 horas, exigir KYC generalizado ni introducir nuevas facultades de confiscación o bloqueo selectivo de retiradas.

Tampoco se presupone que desarrollar nuevos mecanismos sea necesariamente la mejor solución. El estudio deberá comparar estas alternativas con los controles existentes y justificar cualquier complejidad adicional.

Solicitud inicial

Abrir una discusión comunitaria sobre la conveniencia de realizar un estudio de viabilidad con objetivos, entregables, responsables y presupuesto definidos.

El propósito no es detener toda actividad ante una alerta, sino impedir que el riesgo crezca más rápido que la capacidad de evaluarlo y responder.

PARTE II. DOCUMENTO TÉCNICO

2. Contexto y problema identificado

Los protocolos descentralizados permiten realizar operaciones financieras sin depender necesariamente de intermediarios tradicionales.

Esta arquitectura ofrece ventajas importantes en términos de acceso, transparencia y autonomía financiera. Sin embargo, también puede exponer a los protocolos de préstamos a riesgos procedentes de infraestructuras externas.

Aave puede mantener sus contratos inteligentes operativos y, aun así, verse afectado por acontecimientos que comprometan activos aceptados como garantía.

Se identifican dos escenarios principales.

2.1. Deterioro de una garantía

Un ataque contra un protocolo externo puede comprometer el respaldo, la liquidez o la capacidad de recuperación de un activo utilizado como garantía.

Si el mercado continúa permitiendo la generación de nueva deuda mientras se evalúa el incidente, la exposición puede aumentar.

El riesgo consiste en que el valor efectivo de la garantía deje de cubrir adecuadamente las obligaciones respaldadas por ella.

2.2. Utilización de activos relacionados con robos

Un atacante puede intentar utilizar activos obtenidos mediante un incidente de seguridad para depositarlos como garantía y solicitar préstamos en otros activos.

La sobrecolateralización no elimina este riesgo.

Una garantía puede tener suficiente valor de mercado para respaldar un préstamo y, al mismo tiempo, estar vinculada a fondos sustraídos.

Se trata de un problema distinto del deterioro de una garantía: el primero afecta a la procedencia y a las implicaciones legales de los activos; el segundo afecta a la solvencia económica de la posición.

Ambos escenarios merecen ser evaluados, pero no deben recibir automáticamente el mismo tratamiento.

2.3. Pregunta central

¿Puede Aave reducir materialmente su exposición durante un incidente externo mediante controles temporales sobre la nueva capacidad crediticia, sin perjudicar de forma desproporcionada a los usuarios legítimos?

3. Objetivos y principios de diseño

AAVE SECURITY SHIELD establece los siguientes objetivos:

  1. Reducir la exposición acumulada antes de detectar y contener una amenaza.
  2. Limitar la generación acelerada de nueva deuda cuando exista un riesgo verificable.
  3. Preservar las operaciones que permiten reducir el riesgo de las posiciones existentes.
  4. Reutilizar los controles actuales siempre que sea posible.
  5. Evitar restricciones generales cuando una intervención más limitada resulte suficiente.
  6. Mantener facultades de emergencia acotadas, transparentes y supervisadas.
  7. Evaluar los costes y efectos secundarios antes de proponer un despliegue.

Principios fundamentales

Prevención: proporcionar tiempo para evaluar amenazas antes de que se acumule una exposición significativa.

Proporcionalidad: aplicar medidas acordes con la naturaleza y magnitud del riesgo.

Privacidad: evitar la identificación personal universal y limitar el análisis a la información necesaria.

Descentralización: preservar la gobernanza y evitar concentraciones injustificadas de autoridad.

Transparencia: documentar las medidas, sus motivos y sus resultados.

Responsabilidad: no presentar el sistema como una garantía absoluta frente a robos o pérdidas.

4. Relación con los mecanismos actuales de Aave

Antes de introducir nuevas herramientas, es imprescindible analizar qué controles existen en cada versión y mercado del protocolo.

La evaluación deberá estudiar, entre otros:

  • Supply caps.
  • Borrow caps.
  • Borrow y draw restrictions.
  • Loan-to-Value (LTV).
  • Liquidation Threshold.
  • Isolation Mode.
  • Debt Ceilings.
  • Risk Stewards y mecanismos de emergencia.
  • Umbrella y mecanismos de cobertura aplicables.

4.1. Antecedentes operativos

Las actuaciones de los Risk Stewards durante incidentes anteriores, incluido el episodio relacionado con Binance en octubre de 2026, constituyen antecedentes relevantes para esta investigación.

Esas actuaciones permiten estudiar cómo se pueden reducir los límites de exposición y la capacidad de generar nueva deuda sin necesariamente paralizar todas las operaciones.

La propuesta pretende investigar si estos controles pueden complementarse con mecanismos preventivos más estructurados.

4.2. Diferencia entre los controles

Mecanismo

Función principal

Borrow cap

Limitar la deuda total de un activo

Draw cap

Limitar la capacidad disponible para nuevos préstamos

Límites temporales

Controlar la velocidad de generación de deuda

Maduración

Retrasar la habilitación de nuevas garantías

Capacidad gradual

Habilitar progresivamente capacidad de endeudamiento

No se presupone que todas estas herramientas sean nuevas ni que todas deban implementarse.

El estudio deberá determinar qué carencias existen realmente y qué mejoras pueden conseguirse mediante ajustes de los parámetros actuales.

5. Mecanismos preventivos que se propone evaluar

Se estudiarán tres alternativas principales.

5.1. Maduración selectiva de nuevas garantías

Se evaluará la posibilidad de introducir un periodo de maduración antes de que determinados depósitos puedan respaldar nueva deuda.

La aplicación podría variar según:

  • El activo.
  • El mercado.
  • El nivel de riesgo.
  • Las características de la garantía.
  • La exposición existente.

Una espera de 24 horas podrá utilizarse como escenario de simulación, pero no se propone como requisito universal.

El estudio deberá evaluar su eficacia, el impacto sobre la liquidez y las posibles vías de elusión.

5.2. Habilitación gradual de capacidad crediticia

Se estudiará si una nueva garantía puede adquirir capacidad para respaldar deuda de forma progresiva.

Por ejemplo, en lugar de permitir que toda la capacidad de endeudamiento esté disponible inmediatamente, se podría evaluar una habilitación escalonada.

Esto podría reducir la cantidad de exposición que se genera durante los primeros minutos u horas de una operación.

No se propone todavía una fórmula ni una velocidad determinada.

5.3. Límites a la velocidad de endeudamiento

Se propone investigar límites a la cantidad de nueva deuda que puede generarse durante una ventana temporal.

El análisis deberá considerar:

  • Límites por activo utilizado como garantía.
  • Límites por activo prestado.
  • Límites agregados por mercado.
  • Ventanas temporales diferentes.
  • Combinaciones con borrow caps y draw caps.
  • Mecanismos de ajuste durante incidentes.

Una limitación exclusivamente por dirección no sería suficiente, ya que un atacante podría distribuir las operaciones entre múltiples carteras.

Por tanto, el estudio deberá priorizar los límites de exposición agregada y no depender exclusivamente de la identidad o del historial de una cartera.

5.4. Comparación de alternativas

Alternativa

Beneficio esperado

Principal inconveniente

Maduración selectiva

Más tiempo de detección

Retraso para usuarios

Capacidad gradual

Menor exposición inicial

Mayor complejidad

Límites temporales

Menor acumulación de deuda

Posible restricción de liquidez

Se evaluarán por separado y en combinación.

La solución recomendada deberá justificar su ventaja frente a las alternativas existentes.

6. Protección de posiciones existentes

Un aspecto prioritario de la propuesta es evitar que las medidas preventivas generen problemas adicionales a los usuarios que ya tienen préstamos abiertos.

El diseño deberá distinguir entre:

  • Aportar garantía para reducir el riesgo de una posición existente.
  • Aportar garantía para obtener nueva capacidad de endeudamiento.

Siempre que sea técnicamente seguro, se buscará preservar:

  • La devolución de deuda.
  • Las liquidaciones.
  • Las aportaciones de garantía destinadas a reducir el riesgo.
  • Las retiradas compatibles con la solvencia de la posición y la liquidez disponible.

También se estudiará el efecto de las restricciones sobre la utilización de las reservas y los tipos de interés.

No deberá asumirse que detener nuevas operaciones carece de consecuencias para los usuarios existentes.

7. Sistema de alerta y respuesta escalonada

Se propone evaluar un sistema denominado Security Response.

Su objetivo sería permitir una respuesta proporcional ante incidentes externos.

Nivel

Situación

Medida propuesta

1. Observación

Señal no confirmada

Monitorización y análisis

2. Precaución

Evidencia relevante

Evaluación de restricciones a nueva exposición

3. Emergencia

Incidente confirmado con exposición material

Restricciones de nueva deuda dentro de las facultades aprobadas

4. Recuperación

Amenaza contenida

Retirada gradual de restricciones y publicación de resultados

7.1. Fuentes de información

El estudio podrá evaluar la utilización de:

  • Proveedores de análisis blockchain.
  • Informes de protocolos afectados.
  • Investigadores independientes.
  • Equipos de seguridad.
  • Información pública verificable.
  • Sistemas de monitorización de contratos y mercados.

Una alerta aislada de un proveedor privado no deberá bastar automáticamente para activar medidas restrictivas.

7.2. Criterios de activación

Las medidas deberán justificarse mediante:

  1. Calidad de la evidencia.
  2. Alcance del incidente.
  3. Exposición económica potencial.
  4. Relación con los activos afectados.
  5. Riesgo de propagación.
  6. Posibilidad de reducir la exposición mediante controles existentes.

La activación deberá ser proporcional al riesgo y no depender únicamente de una etiqueta de fondos sospechosos.

8. Límites de las facultades de emergencia

La fase inicial no propone nuevas facultades para:

  • Confiscar activos.
  • Transferir fondos de usuarios a terceros.
  • Modificar arbitrariamente saldos.
  • Bloquear selectivamente retiradas por una simple asociación entre direcciones.

Cualquier propuesta futura que amplíe estas facultades deberá tramitarse por separado.

Para las restricciones de nueva exposición que sí se estudien, deberán definirse:

  • Quién puede proponerlas.
  • Quién puede ejecutarlas.
  • Qué acciones están autorizadas.
  • Qué mercados pueden verse afectados.
  • Qué duración pueden tener.
  • Cuándo caducan.
  • Cómo se revisan.
  • Cómo se revocan.
  • Qué información debe publicarse.

Se estudiará un mecanismo de caducidad automática de las nuevas restricciones, con renovación expresa cuando esté justificada.

9. Privacidad y protección de usuarios

AAVE SECURITY SHIELD no contempla imponer identificación personal universal para utilizar Aave.

El análisis deberá centrarse en información pública y señales directamente relacionadas con el riesgo evaluado.

Principios:

  • No exigir DNI o pasaporte de forma universal.
  • No publicar identidades personales.
  • Limitar la recopilación de información.
  • Evitar restricciones basadas exclusivamente en asociaciones indirectas entre carteras.
  • Documentar los motivos de las intervenciones.
  • Establecer mecanismos para corregir falsos positivos.
  • Evitar excepciones discrecionales para usuarios considerados de confianza.

La privacidad y la autonomía financiera deben seguir siendo elementos fundamentales del protocolo.

10. Resiliencia financiera y cobertura de déficits

Se propone estudiar la capacidad de Aave para absorber pérdidas derivadas de incidentes externos.

El análisis deberá coordinarse con los mecanismos existentes, incluido Umbrella cuando corresponda.

Se evaluarán:

  1. Reservas y coberturas disponibles.
  2. Deudas potencialmente incobrables.
  3. Riesgos de concentración.
  4. Dependencias externas.
  5. Capacidad efectiva de cobertura.
  6. Posibles déficits no cubiertos.
  7. Costes de reforzar las reservas existentes.

No se propone crear un fondo adicional sin demostrar previamente su necesidad.

Tampoco se deberá presentar ninguna reserva como una garantía absoluta de los depósitos.

11. Riesgos de implementación

La propuesta reconoce que sus propios mecanismos podrían introducir nuevos problemas.

Falsos positivos

Una operación legítima podría recibir una alerta por su relación indirecta con fondos comprometidos.

Elusión

Un atacante podría utilizar múltiples carteras, intermediarios o diferentes rutas de financiación.

Impacto sobre posiciones existentes

Las restricciones podrían afectar a la capacidad de añadir garantías, retirar fondos o reducir deuda.

Concentración de poder

Una autoridad de emergencia mal diseñada podría introducir riesgos de centralización.

Manipulación

Las alertas falsas podrían utilizarse para provocar restricciones o perjudicar a otros participantes.

Complejidad técnica

Las modificaciones de los procesos de depósito, garantía y préstamo podrían introducir nuevas vulnerabilidades.

Reducción de utilidad

Los controles podrían perjudicar a usuarios legítimos más de lo que protegen al protocolo.

Falsa sensación de seguridad

El sistema podría interpretarse erróneamente como una protección total frente a cualquier ataque.

Todos estos escenarios deberán formar parte de las pruebas.

12. Estudio de viabilidad

La primera fase de AAVE SECURITY SHIELD no solicita modificaciones inmediatas del protocolo.

Solicita evaluar si existe una mejora técnica y económica suficiente para justificar su desarrollo.

Entregables propuestos

  1. Inventario de los controles existentes por versión y mercado.
  2. Identificación de los riesgos que no están suficientemente cubiertos.
  3. Comparación de las tres alternativas preventivas.
  4. Simulaciones retrospectivas de incidentes seleccionados.
  5. Pruebas con escenarios adversos hipotéticos.
  6. Análisis de posibles vías de elusión.
  7. Evaluación de impacto sobre liquidez y usuarios.
  8. Revisión de los mecanismos actuales de cobertura.
  9. Análisis jurídico y de gobernanza de las facultades propuestas.
  10. Estimación de costes.
  11. Recomendación de continuar, modificar o descartar.
  12. Diseño de un posible piloto, únicamente si los resultados lo justifican.

Simulaciones propuestas

Se estudiarán distintos escenarios:

  • Ataque externo con garantía que pierde su respaldo.
  • Utilización de activos vinculados a un robo.
  • Generación rápida de deuda en múltiples carteras.
  • Retirada masiva de depósitos durante una crisis.
  • Falsas alertas contra direcciones legítimas.
  • Incidente que afecta a varios mercados simultáneamente.

Las simulaciones deberán explicar sus supuestos y limitaciones.

No se considerará demostrado que un mecanismo habría evitado una pérdida simplemente porque retrase una operación.

13. Métricas de evaluación

Para determinar si la iniciativa aporta valor, se utilizarán indicadores medibles:

Indicador

Qué permite evaluar

Tiempo de detección

Rapidez para identificar amenazas

Tiempo de respuesta

Rapidez para ejecutar medidas

Exposición restringida

Cantidad de nueva deuda que se evita generar

Pérdidas potenciales

Diferencia estimada entre escenarios

Falsos positivos

Restricciones indebidas

Tiempo de resolución

Duración de las revisiones

Impacto sobre liquidez

Efectos en usuarios y mercados

Coste operativo

Recursos necesarios

Eficacia frente a elusión

Resistencia a estrategias alternativas

Las estimaciones de pérdidas evitadas deberán contar con una metodología transparente y análisis de sensibilidad.

14. Recursos y presupuesto

No se establece una cantidad económica definitiva sin disponer de un alcance técnico y presupuestos verificables.

Las principales áreas de trabajo serían:

Área

Trabajo

Gestión de riesgos

Modelización y simulaciones

Ingeniería

Diseño técnico e integraciones

Seguridad

Auditorías y pruebas adversariales

Operaciones

Monitorización y respuesta

Jurídico

Revisión de facultades y responsabilidades

Gobernanza

Supervisión y transparencia

Mantenimiento

Seguimiento y actualización

La aprobación de un estudio no implicaría la aprobación automática del desarrollo ni del despliegue.

Cualquier presupuesto deberá presentarse de forma separada y con entregables definidos.

15. Plan de implementación

Si el estudio demuestra una mejora suficiente, se propone el siguiente recorrido:

Fase 1. Investigación

Analizar los controles actuales y definir las carencias.

Fase 2. Diseño técnico

Comparar las alternativas y seleccionar las que justifiquen su desarrollo.

Fase 3. Prototipo

Desarrollar una versión experimental sin afectar a los fondos reales de los usuarios.

Fase 4. Auditoría

Realizar auditorías independientes y pruebas de escenarios adversos.

Fase 5. Piloto limitado

Evaluar el sistema en un entorno y alcance justificados.

Fase 6. Evaluación comunitaria

Publicar resultados, costes, riesgos y efectos sobre los usuarios.

Fase 7. Gobernanza

Presentar una propuesta formal de implementación únicamente si existe evidencia suficiente.

16. Criterios de cancelación o rediseño

La iniciativa deberá detenerse o modificarse si:

  • No reduce materialmente la exposición en los escenarios evaluados.
  • Resulta fácilmente eludible.
  • Perjudica desproporcionadamente a los usuarios legítimos.
  • Dificulta operaciones esenciales para reducir riesgos.
  • Requiere facultades de emergencia excesivas.
  • Introduce complejidad injustificada.
  • Puede sustituirse por controles existentes con resultados comparables.
  • Sus costes superan los beneficios esperados.

No implementar el sistema también será un resultado válido del estudio.

17. Gobernanza y recorrido de la propuesta

AAVE SECURITY SHIELD se presenta como una iniciativa comunitaria independiente.

El recorrido recomendado sería:

  1. Presentación de la iniciativa en el Aave Governance Forum.
  2. Discusión pública y recepción de comentarios.
  3. Evaluación preliminar de la comunidad.
  4. Preparación de una posible ARFC para definir el estudio.
  5. Evaluación de alcance, responsables y presupuesto.
  6. Aprobación de la fase de investigación, si corresponde.
  7. Publicación de resultados.
  8. Preparación de una AIP únicamente si se justifican cambios concretos en el protocolo.

La iniciativa no representa oficialmente a Aave DAO ni presupone el apoyo de sus equipos de desarrollo, proveedores de riesgos o delegados.

18. Solicitud a la comunidad

En esta primera fase se solicita a la comunidad valorar cinco cuestiones:

  1. ¿Existe una necesidad de estudiar controles adicionales sobre la velocidad de generación de nueva deuda durante incidentes externos?
  2. ¿Qué mecanismos actuales deberían analizarse antes de introducir otros nuevos?
  3. ¿Qué alternativas merecen una evaluación técnica?
  4. ¿Qué garantías deberían exigirse para proteger a los usuarios y la descentralización?
  5. ¿Qué resultados y condiciones deberían cumplirse antes de autorizar un piloto?

La finalidad de esta primera discusión es determinar si existe interés suficiente para desarrollar un estudio formal.

No se solicita aprobar nuevas restricciones, modificar contratos ni crear facultades de intervención adicionales en esta etapa.

19. Conclusión

AAVE SECURITY SHIELD propone investigar cómo mejorar la prevención y la capacidad de respuesta del protocolo ante incidentes externos.

La iniciativa no pretende eliminar todos los riesgos de DeFi ni convertir Aave en una entidad bancaria tradicional.

Busca evaluar si es posible reducir la velocidad y el volumen de nueva exposición crediticia durante una crisis, preservando al mismo tiempo la privacidad, la autonomía y las operaciones legítimas de los usuarios.

La seguridad debe evolucionar junto con el crecimiento del ecosistema financiero descentralizado.

Principio rector:

«Impedir que el riesgo crezca más rápido que la capacidad del protocolo para evaluarlo y responder».
